title: Stumbling on Happiness
author: Daniel Gilbert
target_audience: Individuals curious about human happiness and decision-making
Students and professionals in psychology, neuroscience, and behavioral economics
Anyone seeking insight into how we predict, perceive, and pursue happiness
core_themes: Inaccuracy of affective forecasting (predicting future happiness)
Limits of imagination and memory when projecting future feelings
Difference between anticipated and experienced happiness
The malleability and unreliability of human perception
primary_purpose: To explore why people are often poor at predicting what will make them happy in the future, to expose psychological illusions and cognitive biases underlying our pursuit of happiness, and to share research that helps us understand—and possibly improve—our quest for fulfillment.

structure_format.narrative_style: Conversational, humorous, narrative-driven with a blend of anecdotes and scientific studies
structure_format.organization: Structured into thematic chapters, each addressing a particular aspect of happiness and prediction
features: Use of wit and humor to engage readers
Endnotes and references for further reading

key_concepts_lessons: Humans consistently overestimate or underestimate how future events will affect their happiness.
Memory and imagination are faulty guides for predicting future emotions.
Cognitive biases such as impact bias and presentism skew our ability to make accurate predictions.
We often ignore the experiences of others, which can actually offer reliable information about possible futures.
True happiness is elusive, not because of external circumstances, but because our minds systematically misjudge what will bring us lasting joy.
notable_features: Illustrated with memorable anecdotes and analogies
cultural_historical_context: Emerging in the mid-2000s alongside the rise of positive psychology and heightened interest in well-being, the book contributed to mainstream understanding of how psychological science can inform our pursuit of happiness.
reception_impact: Bestseller and widely acclaimed for making complex psychological research accessible
Praised for its humor and clarity
Influential among both lay audiences and professionals in psychology and behavioral economics
Cited in numerous academic and popular discussions about happiness and decision science
comparable_titles: The Happiness Hypothesis by Jonathan Haidt
Thinking, Fast and Slow by Daniel Kahneman
The Art of Happiness by Dalai Lama and Howard Cutler
